units.translation: Hesychius ἀθήρ [awn, spear-point]: ἐπιδορατίς [spear-head]. Metaphorically in Aeschylus' Nereids. Bekker's Anecdota p. 353, 16 ἀθήρ [awn, spear-point]: ἀκμὴ τοῦ ἠκονημένου σιδήρου [the point of sharpened iron], by metaphor from ἀθένος [the awn], that is, of the ear of corn. The spear-head is also called ἀθήρ [awn, spear-point].

Absurdly written in M as ἄφυκτον [unavoidable] where the sense demands the opposite. I have corrected it to ἄθικτον [untouched], with which can be compared Ag. 432 πολλὰ γοῦν θιγγάνει πρὸς παρ [many things indeed touch against...].
the water of the Nile untouched by diseases
and no longer would the heart be untouched
for whom the grace of things untouched may be trodden
I shall toil for a time of ten thousand years
and it is possible to speak upon wretched things
wretched Io, driven by the gadfly
may he grant you a contest more painful than this
the greatest contest of her father, covering the sky
seek some release from the contest
and when the multitude of ships was gathered in the narrow strait
to be disheartened, to lose heart
to be disheartened, to lose heart
having fallen into sickness, you are disheartened
not as a spiritless man nor with cowardice of spirit

In M Αθωον [Athoan]. For some grammarians (as Choeroboscus in Etym. M. s. h. v.) decided to write "A wos" or at least Αθώος [Athoan] without the iota subscript, in order to distinguish it from ἀθῷος [unpunished].
The tragedians do not use this form except where the meter does not allow γαῖα [earth]. There are many examples of it in Aeschylus and Euripides, only two in Sophocles. These are the Aeschylean ones.
where Hermann corrected Ελλανίδος γᾶς [of the Greek land] for the sake of the meter.
I have restored the defective verse, where a trimeter is required, as follows
to come to the iron-mother earth
to the land, the Greek country
the common sea-washed headland of both lands
all the land through which the holy Strymon flows
through the sheep-pasturing land of Phrygia
who has come to this boundary hill of the land
and the land laments its native youth
an interjection by which grief or pain is expressed
